<header>The Chapter on Impurity</header>

250. But for one in whom this <note>the tendency to lie, slandering, and other vices mentioned in previous verses</note> is entirely cut off, uprooted, and destroyed, that person truly attains composure of mind <term>samādhi</term> <gloss>concentration or meditative stabilization</gloss> by day and by night.
8. The Story of the Novice Tissa <note>original: Tissa dāharassa vatthu; see Commentary volume III, page 357</note>

251. There is no fire like lust <term>rāga</term> <gloss>passion or attachment</gloss>; there is no grip like hatred <term>dosa</term> <gloss>aversion or ill-will</gloss>. There is no net like delusion <term>moha</term> <gloss>ignorance or confusion</gloss>; there is no river like craving <term>taṇhā</term> <gloss>thirst or desire</gloss>.
9. The Story of the Five Lay Followers <note>original: Pañca-upāsakānaṃ vatthu; see Commentary volume III, page 360</note>

252. The faults of others are easily seen, but one's own are difficult to perceive. A person winnows the faults of others like chaff, but hides their own faults like a dishonest gambler hides an unlucky die <note>original: kali</note>.
10. The Story of Meṇḍaka the Merchant <note>original: Meṇḍakasetthissa vatthu; see Commentary volume III, page 363</note>

253. In one who constantly observes the faults of others and is always seeking to blame them, the mental taints <term>āsavā</term> <gloss>cankers, corruptions, or fermentations</gloss> increase. Such a person is far from the destruction of these taints.
11. The Story of the Elder Who Always Blamed Others <note>original: Ujjhānasaññimattherassa vatthu; see Commentary volume III, page 376</note>

254. There is no footprint in the sky. There is no true recluse <term>samaṇo</term> <gloss>ascetic or seeker</gloss> outside the Path. Humankind delights in worldly obstacles <term>papañca</term> <gloss>conceptual proliferation or mental complications</gloss>, but the Perfected Ones <term>Tathāgatā</term> <gloss>those who have thus gone or thus come, an epithet for the Buddhas</gloss> are free from such obstacles.

255. There is no footprint in the sky. There is no true recluse outside the Path. No conditioned things <term>saṅkhārā</term> <gloss>mental formations or compounded phenomena</gloss> are eternal. There is no instability <term>iñjita</term> <gloss>agitation or movement</gloss> in the Awakened Ones.
12. The Story of Subhadda the Wandering Ascetic <note>original: Subhaddaparibbājakassa vatthu; see Commentary volume III, page 377</note>

->CHAPTER XVIII: THE CHAPTER ON IMPURITY IS FINISHED<-

<note>Footnotes from the original manuscript:</note>
<note>1. Burmese edition reads "kaḷi va" <gloss>as the unlucky die</gloss>. 2. F and C editions read "va" <gloss>as</gloss>; Burmese edition reads "va".</note>
<note>3. K and F editions read "bāhiro" <gloss>outside</gloss>; Burmese and Sinhalese editions read "bāhire" <gloss>in the outside</gloss>.</note>
<note>Reference for verse 252: Jātaka volume III, page 223.</note>

<summary>This page concludes the Chapter on Impurity, providing verses on the destruction of vices, the metaphors for passion and delusion, and the hypocrisy of judging others. It emphasizes that true spiritual seekers and Buddhas are distinguished by their freedom from mental complications and instability.</summary>
<keywords>Dhammapada, Malavaggo, Tissa, lust, hatred, delusion, craving, faults, mental taints, asava, Tathagata, Subhadda, impermanence</keywords>
